title: Service of the heart (Taanit 2a)
hook: the Talmud calls prayer the service of the heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, vayifga, and the three hinges of the day: morning, afternoon, evening. Today, what prayer is, in two Hebrew words.

The Shema, said morning and evening, includes a paragraph from Deuteronomy asking people to serve God with all their heart. Serve how? You can serve with your hands: build, carry, cook, bring an offering to an altar. That's what service meant in the Temple, real physical work. But you can't hand someone your heart on a plate. The Talmud stops at that phrase and asks exactly that question.
screen: `SERVE WITH YOUR HANDS.` → `BUILD, CARRY, COOK, OFFER.` → `BUT WITH YOUR HEART?`

segments.voice: The verse is Deuteronomy eleven: "to love the LORD your God, and to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul." At the opening of tractate Taanit, the Talmud asks: what is service that is in the heart? Its answer: this is prayer. Avodah shebalev, service of the heart. Avodah is the same word used for the priests' work in the Temple: the offerings, the incense, the daily routine. So the phrase makes a bold claim. Prayer is real service, standing alongside the Temple's. After the Temple was destroyed, that idea carried enormous weight: there was still a service anyone could bring, every day, with no altar at all. And the heart? The rabbis learned much about prayer from Hannah, at the start of the book of Samuel, praying for a child. "Now Hannah, she spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice could not be heard." From her, the Talmud learns that prayer needs the heart directed, the lips moving, and the voice kept low. Directing the heart has its own word: kavanah, intention. The siddur supplies the words; the heart does the work of meaning them. That's why it's called service. It isn't only a feeling. It's effort, like any other work.
screen: `SERVE WITH ALL YOUR HEART.` · `AVODAH: THE TEMPLE'S WORK.` · `SERVICE WITHOUT AN ALTAR.` · `HANNAH: LIPS MOVING, VOICE UNHEARD.` · then, large: `PRAYER IS THE HEART'S WORK.`

segments.voice: Let one honest sentence rise in you: thanks, a worry, a hope, a name. Say it the way Hannah did, lips moving, voice barely there, then once more, slower, meaning every word. If you pray, it can be to God in your own words; if not, say it to the quiet.
Avodah shebalev. Service of the heart. The Talmud's name for prayer.
Your line: prayer is the heart's work. The siddur gives the words, and the meaning is yours to bring. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish law asks for kavanah, focused intention, especially in the first line of the Shema and the first blessing of the Amidah, which is said quietly, lips moving, in the manner learned from Hannah.

chat.says: If prayer is just saying words, why does the Talmud call it service?
options: Meaning the words is real work; the Talmud calls prayer service of the heart.
It's called service because in Temple times only the priests were allowed to pray.
Only prayers said aloud in the Temple ever counted as real service.
chat.meaning: Taanit 2a reads serve Him with all your heart as prayer; avodah is the Temple's word for work, so directing the heart is effort.
